newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector reaches wage pact.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector reaches wage pact.

text.p: German chemical employers and union leaders said Wednesday they had reached a 1997 wage agreement for some 590,000 workers in the industry after talks lasting 23 hours.
Negotiators for both sides said the accord included a 1.5 percent pay rise for next year and maintained sick pay entitlements at 100 percent of full salary.

The agreement follows fierce resistance by workers to a new law which allows employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent of salary and which has disturbed the usually comfortable labour relations in the German chemical industry.
Under the agreed package, the existing "thirteenth month" year-end bonus for workers is to be reduced from 100 percent of a month's salary to 95 percent.

Part of the savings from the reduction of the year-end bonus can, on a voluntary basis within individual companies, be used on measures aimed at reducing absenteeism in the sector, employer and union negotiators said.
Employers also committed themselves to providing at least the same number of trainee positions open in the industry for 1997 as were available this year.

Chemical employers such as BASF AG had earlier sought to implement the new sick pay law, which was introduced in October as part of the Bonn government's austerity measures ahead of the single European currency.
But after workers held walk-outs against the move they were forced to back down and begin early negotiations for the 1997 pay round, which would normally begin next spring.
